newsitem.title: UK: Homeowners rush to fix mortgages ahead of UK poll.
newsitem.headline: Homeowners rush to fix mortgages ahead of UK poll.

text.p: Britain's homeowners are rushing to fix mortgage interest rates ahead of Thursday's parliamentary election, amid mounting speculation that once the hustings are over interest rates will rise.
"Predominantly every rate I have done recently on new mortgages has been fixed rate," said Mike Cleaver at Independent Financial Advisers Axiom. "And existing mortgage holders are tending to fix."

"People are snapping up five year fixed rate deals. To an extent it's due to the press warning of higher rates the other side of polling day, but there is a real feeling out there that higher rates are on the way and people are looking for security."
The housing market is currently in the process of emerging from a deep recession, having been pole-axed by the punitive interest rate policy which followed the blow-off boom of the late 1980s.

The Halifax Building Society, Britain's largest mortgage lender, said only around 20 percent of its total mortgage business was fixed rate. But they had seen a pick up this business in the past few weeks.
"I wouldn't say it was a rush into fixed rates but we have seen an upturn in the past few weeks," said a Halifax spokeswoman.
British bank Abbey National has already withdrawn its 6.99 percent deal fixed until July 2002, "Due to the popularity of the fixed rate..."
A telephone operator at the same bank who helps arrange fixed rate deals said on Tuesday the real rush began only in the middle of last week.
"Around last Wednesday it started getting extremely busy with people calling to fix their rates," she said.
"We have around 50 people manning the phones and most of the time there are around 30 customers waiting."

Latest opinion polls show Tony Blair's opposition Labour party 22 points ahead of John Major's ruling Conservatives. If such polls are correct Labour will win with a massive 265-parliamentary majority.
City analysts say whoever wins the election 6.00 percent base rates are likely to rise in the near-term to head off inflationary pressure.

In the event of a Labour win, which would end 18-years of Conservative rule, there is speculation that the new Chancellor, Gordon Brown, could lean towards a tighter monetary stance in order to calm down possible jitters in financial markets.
The latest Reuters poll of interest rate expectations showed financial experts anticipate base rates at 6.75 percent by the end of this year.

Financial advisers also said pensions business has picked up due to concern that a Labour government could change higher rate tax relief on pensions. This had led to people paying single premiums into pensions schemes now to lock in the current higher rate tax relief, they said.
